preview_text: ในการแพทย์แผนจีน อาการแดงที่เต้านมเป็นเรื่องของความร้อนที่ติดอยู่ และระยะของความร้อนนั้นบอกเราอย่างชัดเจนว่าจะรักษาอย่างไร รอยแดงในช่วงต้นมักจะหายไปภายในไม่กี่วันด้วยสมุนไพรที่ช่วยให้...
synonyms: ["Erythematous Breast", "Red Breast", "Breast skin warm to touch or slightly red", "Redness and Warmth of the Breast Skin", "Breast Heat", "Breast Warmth", "Heat Sensation In The Breast", "Hot Breast", "Hot Sensation In The Breast", "Warm Breast", "Burning Sensation In The Mammary Region", "Feeling Of Heat On The Breasts", "Sensation Of Heat In The Breasts"]
conventional_description: In Western medicine, breast redness is most often associated with mastitis - inflammation of the breast tissue, commonly occurring during breastfeeding when a milk duct becomes blocked and infected. It can also arise from non-lactational causes such as periductal mastitis, inflammatory breast cancer (rare but serious), or skin infections. Diagnosis is typically based on physical examination, and if an abscess is suspected, ultrasound is used to confirm fluid collection. Standard treatment includes antibiotics, anti-inflammatory medications, and, if an abscess has formed, drainage.
conventional_treatments: Acute bacterial mastitis is usually treated with a course of antibiotics, continued milk removal (breastfeeding or pumping), and pain relief with ibuprofen or acetaminophen. If an abscess forms, needle aspiration or surgical incision and drainage may be necessary. For recurrent or non-infectious breast redness, further workup is done to rule out underlying conditions.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, the breast is traversed by the Liver and Stomach channels. The Liver channel runs through the nipple area, and the Stomach channel passes through the breast. When emotional stress or frustration causes Liver Qi to stagnate, the flow of Qi and fluids in the breast becomes congested. That stuck Qi can generate Heat, which rises along the channel and inflames the local tissue - this is the first pattern, Liver Qi Stagnation transforming into Heat, where redness is mild to moderate, and the breast feels distended and warm.
If the stagnation is not relieved, the Heat intensifies and transforms into Toxic-Heat. This is a more severe stage where toxins attack the breast tissue, causing a deep, burning redness, throbbing pain, and pus formation. The body's fluids are damaged, and an abscess may develop. This pattern is the TCM equivalent of an acute, full-blown mastitis that is moving toward suppuration.
A third pattern, Qi and Blood Deficiency, often appears after the acute heat has subsided - for example, after an abscess has been drained or after a prolonged bout of inflammation. The body's reserves are depleted, so the breast remains slightly red, swollen, and slow to heal. The redness is dull, not fiery, and the person feels exhausted and pale. This pattern explains why some women have lingering redness and poor wound healing long after the infection is gone.
classical_quote: 「乳痈者，由新产后，儿未能饮，乳汁蓄结，与血气相搏，蕴积生热，故令乳肿，焮赤疼痛。」
classical_translation: "Mastitis occurs after childbirth when the infant cannot suckle, causing milk to accumulate and bind with Qi and Blood, generating heat, which leads to breast swelling, redness, and pain."
classical_source:
Zhu Bing Yuan Hou Lun (Treatise on the Causes and Symptoms of Diseases)  ,  Chapter on Breast Abscess (乳痈候) 									·
More references
tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by asking how the redness started and what it feels like. Acute mastitis (乳痈, rǔ yōng) often follows a blocked milk duct, stress, or dietary heat. The timeline and severity of the redness - whether it is a mild flush or a fiery, burning red - are the first clues that steer the diagnosis toward one pattern over another.
If the redness appeared suddenly, with breast distension, a hard lump, and a sensation of heat that is not yet scalding, the pattern is usually Liver Qi Stagnation transforming into Heat. The person often feels irritable, thirsty, and may have a slight fever with chills. The tongue is red with a thin white or thin yellow coating, and the pulse feels floating and rapid or wiry and rapid.
When the redness deepens to a scorching, fiery red and the lump becomes intensely painful and begins to soften, Toxic-Heat has taken hold. This pattern signals abscess formation. The tongue turns red with a thick yellow, greasy coat, and the pulse becomes flooding and rapid. Pus may start to drain, but the discharge is often incomplete and the skin remains hot.
A less common picture emerges when the acute heat has subsided but the redness lingers low‑grade, with a pale complexion and deep tiredness. This is Qi and Blood Deficiency, seen after prolonged infection or surgical drainage. The tongue is pale with a thin coat, and the pulse is thready. The body lacks the strength to fully clear the remaining heat toxin and close the wound.

patterns.pattern_name: Liver Qi Stagnation that transforms into Heat
patterns.symptoms: ["One-sided breast redness and distending pain", "Irritability and explosive anger", "Bitter taste in mouth", "Symptoms flare with emotional stress"]
patterns.worse_with: Emotional stress, Spicy, greasy, or fried foods, Alcohol, Overwork and lack of rest
patterns.better_with: Gentle breast massage, Warm compress, Rest and calm, Cooling foods and drinks
patterns.why_this_happens: The Liver channel runs through the breast, so when emotional stress and frustration cause Liver Qi to stagnate, the breast area becomes congested. That stuck Qi eventually generates Heat, which rises along the channel and inflames the local tissue, leading to redness, swelling, and distending pain. This is the early, pre-abscess stage of acute mastitis, where the blockage is still primarily Qi-level with Heat beginning to brew.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, redder at the sides, with a thin to moderate yellow coating. Pulse: wiry and rapid (xian shu), especially at the left middle position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Emotional stress is the primary driver of Liver Qi stagnation, which is the root of this pattern; when Qi gets stuck, Heat builds and inflames the breast. Spicy, greasy foods and alcohol add Heat directly to the body, worsening the redness and pain. Gentle massage and warmth help move the stagnant Qi and milk, relieving the blockage, while cooling foods and rest calm the Heat and allow the Liver to smooth out its flow.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, greasy, and fried foods, as well as alcohol, which all add Heat. Eat more cooling greens like dandelion leaves and cucumber. Gentle breast massage toward the nipple, followed by warm compresses, can help move stagnant milk. Prioritize emotional calm-deep breathing and short walks reduce Liver tension.

patterns.worse_with: Spicy, greasy, or fried foods, Alcohol, Emotional stress and anger, Overwork and lack of rest
patterns.better_with: Cooling herbal compresses, Rest and calm, Cooling foods and drinks
patterns.why_this_happens: When early breast congestion is not resolved, stagnant Qi and milk turn into intense heat toxins. These toxins attack the local tissues, causing the breast to become deep red, burning hot, and throbbing with pain. The heat damages flesh and fluids, leading to pus formation and abscess development.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with prickly thorns and a dry yellow coating. Pulse: rapid (数 shuò), forceful, and full (实 shí).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Spicy and greasy foods generate internal heat and dampness, which directly feed the toxic-heat fire. Alcohol is pure heat that aggravates inflammation. Emotional stress stirs Liver Qi, which can transform into fire and worsen breast congestion. Cooling compresses and foods help drain heat from the local area and the body, while rest conserves Qi to fight the infection.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid all spicy, greasy, and fried foods, as well as alcohol, which add fuel to the fire. Eat cooling, detoxifying foods like mung beans, watermelon, cucumber, and dandelion greens. Rest is essential; overexertion depletes Qi and allows heat to deepen. If an abscess has formed, seek professional drainage; do not attempt to squeeze it yourself.

patterns.worse_with: Overwork and lack of rest, Emotional stress, Cold, raw foods, Prolonged illness

patterns.why_this_happens: After a bout of acute mastitis or abscess, the body's Qi and Blood are drained. Without enough Qi to drive out lingering pathogens and enough Blood to nourish tissue, the breast remains slightly red, swollen, and slow to heal. The redness is dull and low-grade, not fiery, and often accompanied by a thin, watery discharge rather than thick pus. This is a state of deficiency, where the body lacks the resources to fully recover.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale body, may be thin or have teeth marks, with a thin white coating. Pulse: fine and weak, especially in the right Guan position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: This pattern is rooted in Qi and Blood deficiency. Rest and nourishing foods replenish the body's resources, giving it the strength to heal and clear lingering pathogens. Overwork and emotional stress further deplete Qi, while cold foods weaken the Spleen, hampering recovery.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, nourishing foods like congee with red dates and goji berries, bone broth, and steamed vegetables. Avoid raw, cold, and greasy foods that weaken the Spleen. Rest as much as possible and avoid overexertion. Gentle breast massage with warm compresses can help clear residual stagnation.

faqs.question: Can TCM help with breast redness during breastfeeding?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM is particularly well-suited for lactation-related breast redness because it can clear the underlying milk stasis and Heat without interrupting breastfeeding. Herbal formulas like Gua Lou Niu Bang Zi Tang are designed to unblock milk ducts and reduce inflammation while being safe for nursing mothers. Acupuncture can also be used to relieve pain and promote milk flow. Always inform your practitioner that you are breastfeeding so they can select the safest herbs.

faqs.question: How quickly can herbs reduce breast redness?
faqs.answer: In the early stage, when redness is mild and there is no pus, many women notice a reduction in redness and pain within 2-3 days of starting herbal treatment. If redness is severe and an abscess is forming, it may take a week or more to see significant improvement, and TCM is often combined with conventional care. Herbal treatment continues even after the redness fades to prevent recurrence.

faqs.question: Can I use TCM alongside antibiotics for mastitis?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM and antibiotics can be used together safely. In fact, many patients find that herbs help resolve the underlying congestion and reduce pain while the antibiotics address the infection. Tell both your TCM practitioner and your doctor about all medications and herbs you are taking. Certain herbs that strongly move Blood or clear Heat should be monitored if you are on blood-thinning medications, but typical mastitis formulas are generally compatible with antibiotics.

faqs.question: Is acupuncture safe if I have an abscess?
faqs.answer: Acupuncture can be helpful for pain relief and reducing inflammation even when an abscess is present, but needles are never inserted directly into the abscess or infected tissue. A skilled practitioner will use distal points on the arms, legs, and back to clear Heat and support healing. If the abscess requires drainage, that should be done by a medical doctor; acupuncture can support recovery afterward.

faqs.question: What if I have recurrent breast redness?
faqs.answer: Recurrent redness suggests an underlying constitutional imbalance - often Liver Qi stagnation with Heat or Qi and Blood Deficiency - that was not fully resolved after the first episode. TCM can identify and correct that tendency, reducing the frequency and severity of future flare-ups. Treatment between episodes focuses on smoothing Liver Qi, strengthening the Spleen and Stomach, and building Qi and Blood.

faqs.question: Will I need to change my diet?
faqs.answer: Dietary adjustments are an important part of TCM treatment for breast redness. In general, you'll be advised to avoid spicy, greasy, and deep-fried foods, as well as alcohol, because they generate internal Heat and Dampness. Instead, focus on cooling, light foods like mung beans, cucumber, watermelon, and plenty of green vegetables. If your pattern involves Qi and Blood Deficiency, warm, nourishing foods like bone broth and congee are recommended once the acute redness subsides.

research.title: Chinese Herbal Medicine for Acute Mastitis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
research.description: This systematic review of randomized controlled trials evaluated Chinese herbal medicine for acute mastitis. It found that herbal formulas like Gua Lou Niu Bang Zi Tang and Wu Wei Xiao Du Yin significantly improved cure rates and reduced pain and swelling compared to antibiotics alone, with fewer adverse events.
research.periodical: Zhao, C., et al. (2016). Chinese Herbal Medicine for Acute Mastitis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine, 2016, 8923134.

research.title: Acupuncture for lactation mastitis: a case series
research.description: This case series reported on acupuncture treatment for women with lactation mastitis. After a few sessions of acupuncture at points including Rugen ST-18 and Quchi LI-11, most participants experienced rapid relief of breast pain, redness, and fever, with no adverse effects on breastfeeding.
research.periodical: Kvist, L. J., et al. (2007). Acupuncture for lactation mastitis: a case series. Acupuncture in Medicine, 25(4), 188-192.
